## Proof

Let $(x, y) = \alpha$. We use the convention that the inner product is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second. Then

$$\|x + cy\|^2 = (x+cy,\, x+cy) = \|x\|^2 + \bar{c}\,\alpha + c\,\bar{\alpha} + |c|^2\|y\|^2.$$

The hypothesis $\|x\| \le \|x+cy\|$ for all $c \in \mathbb{C}$ is equivalent to

$$\bar{c}\,\alpha + c\,\bar{\alpha} + |c|^2\|y\|^2 \ge 0 \quad \text{for all } c \in \mathbb{C}. \tag{$\ast$}$$

Write $\alpha = |\alpha|e^{i\theta}$ and choose $c = t\,e^{i\theta}$ with $t \in \mathbb{R}$. Then $\bar{c} = t\,e^{-i\theta}$, so

$$\bar{c}\,\alpha = t\,e^{-i\theta}\cdot|\alpha|e^{i\theta} = t|\alpha|, \qquad c\,\bar{\alpha} = t\,e^{i\theta}\cdot|\alpha|e^{-i\theta} = t|\alpha|.$$

Thus ($\ast$) becomes

$$2t|\alpha| + t^2\|y\|^2 \ge 0 \quad \text{for all } t \in \mathbb{R}.$$

Setting $t = -s$ for $s > 0$ gives

$$-2s|\alpha| + s^2\|y\|^2 \ge 0 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad s\|y\|^2 \ge 2|\alpha| \quad \text{for all } s > 0.$$

Letting $s \to 0^+$, the left-hand side tends to $0$, so we must have $2|\alpha| \le 0$, i.e. $|\alpha| = 0$. Hence $\alpha = (x, y) = 0$.

### PROOF COMPLETE
